newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Identifying the doubtful budget measures.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Identifying the doubtful budget measures.

text.p: The Labor Opposition and the Australian Democrats have both published over the past week lists of budget measures that they oppose.
Items on both lists now become the focus of Senate action. If three of the remaining four non-government senators back Labor and the Democrats in opposing a measure, it will not go through.

So a theoretical maximum fiscal impact of parliament action can now be calculated: measures worth A$1.248 billion in 1997/98 are at stake, compared with a forecast budget tightening of A$7.152 billion in that year.
Note that the figure is only a maximum.
Here are the measures that both the Labor Party and the Australian Democrats say they will certainly oppose.

The analysis focuses on the gain to the budget from each measure in 1997/98, the first year in which most of them have a substantial effect, and in 1999/00, when they have typically reached full value:

-- Pharmaceutical benefit scheme charges. The government wants people to pay more for each prescription: A$3.20 for low-income earners, A$20 for everyone else. Value: A$134 million in 1997/98, A$147 million in 1999/00.

-- Court fees. Labor opposes the government's plan to raise fees in all Federal tribunals, but the Democrats are against only higher fees in the Family Court. Value: less than A$27 million in 1997/98 (the gain if fees rose in all courts) or less than A$31 million (1999/00).
-- Student charges. The government wants to hike the charges for some university courses for new students. Value: A$66 million in 1997/98, A$123 million in 1999/00.

-- Student charges repayments. Students can defer payment of their charges until their income reaches a certain threshhold. The government wants to drop that threshhold, initiating faster repayments. Value: A$230 million in 1997/98, A$318 million.

-- Medical expenses rebate. People whose medical expenses exceed A$1000 a year get a tax rebate, depending on their income. The government wants to raise the income threshhold. Value: A$26 million in 1997/98, A$24 million in 1999/00.
-- TOTAL: A$483 million in 1997/98; A$643 million in 1999/00.
In addition, the Democrats say their vote on some other issues is subject to negotiation. The items that Labor definitely opposes and which the Democrats want to talk about are:

-- Research and development tax break. Companies can deduct 150 percent of R&D spending from taxable income. The government wants to cut this to 125 percent. Value: A$430 million in 1997/98, A$440 million in 1999/00.
-- Childcare subsidies. The government wants to tighten eligibility. Value: A$147 million in 1997/98, A$170 million in 1999/00.
-- Nursing home charges. The government wants residents to pay more, as they do in other forms of accommodation for the aged. Value: A$125 million in 1997/98, A$194 million in 1999/00.
-- Student income support ("Austudy"). The government wants to tighten eligibility, in part by commencing elligibility at a greater age. Value: A$63 million in 1997/98; A$78 million in 1999/00.
-- TOTAL: A$765 million in 1997/98, A$882 million in 1999/00.

The grand total value of measures which the Labor party will oppose and which the Democrats might oppose is A$1.248 billion in 1997/98 (compared with a forecast budget tightening of A$7.2 billion) and A$1.525 billion in 1999/00.
These figures, then, represent the maximum possible impact of parliamentary action on the budget.
The actual effect will no doubt be much less, since the Democrats may well let through some of the items they say are subject to negotiation.
Moreover, the other senators, particularly the two Indpendents, may back some of the items which both the Democrats and Labor oppose.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
